newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges rebels in Zaire to end abuses.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges rebels in Zaire to end abuses.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday urged Tutsi rebels in Zaire to end political murders and other human rights abuses against refugees returning to Rwanda.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the message was given to rebel leader Laurent Kabila by the acting deputy chief of mission of the U.S. embassy in Kinshasa.

"The message was essentially the following. The United States is deeply concerned about the allegations of political murders and human rights abuses in eastern Zaire by elements of the rebel alliance," Burns said at his daily briefing.

"We are calling on the rebel leaders to act immediately to investigate all reports of human rights abuses, to halt any operations that would take the life or victimise the innocent civilians who are trying to make their way back to Rwanda."

Burns said Washington also asked the rebel leaders to bring those responsible for the killings and human rights abuses to justice and to open up areas of eastern Zaire under their control to international monitors.
He said the United States opposed any partition of Zaire such as creation of a Tutsi-ruled state.

"The United States will not support in any way, shape, or form any effort by the rebel alliance to try to create any kind of artificial state in eastern Zaire or to deny to the government of Zaire its responsibilities in maintaining the international border with Rwanda and the other countries in central Africa and east Africa," Burns said.

Earlier, Richard Bogosian, the department's coordinator for Rwanda and Burundi, told a House hearing that the United States remains open to joining an international force to help refugees in central Africa if it has a clear mission.

"We remain open-minded to a multinational force operation with a clearly defined mission," Bogosian told the House International Relations Committee. "On the other hand, we do not want to commit to an operation without knowing, for example, the whereabouts of the target population, just for the sake of 'doing something.'"

President Bill Clinton said several weeks ago that the United States would be willing to send some 4,000 troops as part of a multinational force in eastern Zaire to help get food and supplies to an estimated 1.1 million refugees fleeing the border into the Zairian interior.
But many of those refugees -- Washington has said 600,000 -- have since returned to Rwanda, throwing plans for the international force into disarray.

Phyllis Oakley, the assistant secretary of state for refugees, said it was believed between 200,000 and 400,000 refugees from the Zairian camps were unaccounted for, though reliable numbers were hard to obtain.
She said there were also more than 700,000 refugees in Tanzania from Rwanda, Burundi and Zaire.

Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Vincent Kern said 446 U.S. military personnel were in the area including 328 in Entebbe, 22 in Kigali and 96 in Mombasa. He said the Pentagon was making plans for airdrops of food and humanitarian supplies if that became necessary.
Bogosian said Washington would back an international conference to resolve the conflicts in central Africa.
